title: The Day Jacob Built a Pillar
paragraphs:
The Day Jacob Built a Pillar
The Stone He Set Up Was Not the Miracle—The God Who Met Him There Was
There are moments in life when everything you built your identity on collapses.
Not because you planned it.
Not because you wanted it.
But because God refuses to leave you as the person you used to be.
Jacob knew that feeling.
Most people remember him as the deceiver.
The manipulator.
The younger brother who stole what belonged to someone else.
His very name carried the weight of scandal.

In Hebrew, יַעֲקֹב (Ya'aqov) comes from a root connected to "heel-grabber" and by extension someone who supplants or takes another's place. From birth, he entered the world grasping his brother Esau's heel (Genesis 25:26).
Jacob's story did not begin with honor.
It began with struggle.
It began with dysfunction.
It began with family wounds.
It began with mistakes that seemed too large to escape.
Maybe that's why so many people see themselves in him.
Because some of us know what it feels like to carry a past we wish nobody knew.
Some of us know what it feels like to be defined by our worst decisions.
Some of us know what it feels like to wake up every morning wondering if God can really use someone like us.
Jacob knew.
And then one night changed everything.
Fleeing from the consequences of his actions, exhausted, uncertain, and completely alone, Jacob stopped to rest.
No choir sang.
No angels announced his arrival.
No one knew where he was.
Yet heaven knew exactly where he was.
Scripture says:
"Then he dreamed, and behold, a ladder was set up on the earth, and its top reached to heaven." (Genesis 28:12)
The Hebrew word translated "ladder" is סֻלָּם (sullam), a rare word appearing only here in Scripture. It describes a connection between heaven and earth.
Jacob was running.
God was pursuing.
Jacob thought he had reached the end of his future.
God was just beginning to reveal it.
As angels ascended and descended, the LORD stood above and spoke promises that stretched beyond Jacob's failures.
Promises he had not earned.
Promises he did not deserve.
Promises rooted entirely in God's grace.
When Jacob awoke, he was shaken.
Not because he had seen angels.
Not because he had experienced something supernatural.
But because he suddenly realized God had been present where he least expected Him.
Genesis 28:16 records his response:
"Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it."
How many people are living that verse right now?
How many are surrounded by evidence of God's mercy yet cannot see it through their pain?
How many are convinced God abandoned them while He is quietly sustaining them?
How many are waiting for a miracle while standing in the middle of one?
Jacob had nothing.
No palace.
No throne.
No inheritance in his hands.
No visible proof that the promises would come true.
Only a stone.
The same stone he had used as a pillow.
The same stone beneath his head while he slept.
The same stone present when heaven interrupted his story.
And then Jacob did something remarkable.
Scripture says:
"So Jacob rose early in the morning, and took the stone that he had put under his head and set it up for a pillar and poured oil on top of it." (Genesis 28:18)
The Hebrew word for pillar is מַצֵּבָה (matzevah).
It was a memorial.
A witness.
A testimony.
Not worship of the stone.
Not superstition.
Not idolatry.
The pillar was a visible reminder of an invisible encounter.
Jacob understood something many people forget.
When God changes your life, you must remember what He has done.
Because there will be future battles.
Future fears.
Future nights when doubt returns.
Future seasons when the promise feels distant.
The pillar was not for God.
The pillar was for Jacob.
A testimony saying:
"I was here."
"God met me here."
"I will never be the same."
Years later, after failures, heartbreaks, fears, wrestling, and transformation, God would bring Jacob back to Bethel.
Back to the place where grace first interrupted his running.
Back to the place where heaven touched earth.
Back to the place where scandal began turning into redemption.
Because that is how God works.
He does not erase your story.
He rewrites it.
The greatest transformation in Jacob's life did not happen because he became stronger.
It happened because he encountered God.
Eventually Jacob would wrestle with the LORD and receive a new name.
יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yisra'el).
Israel.
A new identity.
A new future.
A new story.
The man known for grabbing heels became the father of a nation.
The deceiver became a patriarch.
The fugitive became part of God's redemptive plan.
The scandal became grace.
This pattern reaches its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
When Nathanael first encountered Jesus, something extraordinary happened.
Jesus referenced Jacob's ladder.
In John 1:51 He said:
"Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man."
The Greek text reads:

ἀναβαίνοντας καὶ καταβαίνοντας τοὺς ἀγγέλους τοῦ Θεοῦ
(anabainontas kai katabainontas tous angelous tou Theou)
"the angels of God ascending and descending."
Jesus was declaring something breathtaking.
Jacob saw a ladder connecting heaven and earth.
Jesus revealed that He Himself is that connection.
He is the bridge.
He is the meeting place.
He is Bethel in human flesh.
Bethel means "House of God."
Yet Scripture tells us that in Christ:
"the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14).
The Greek says:

Καὶ ὁ Λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
(Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto)
"And the Word became flesh."
God came down.
He entered our scandal.
He stepped into our brokenness.
He carried our shame.
He bore our sin.
He died our death.
He rose again.
Not so that perfect people could be saved.
But so that sinners could become sons and daughters.
That is why Jacob's pillar still speaks.
Not because the stone was sacred.
But because it points beyond itself.
It points to every place where grace found someone who thought they were beyond saving.
Maybe your pillar is a hospital room.
Maybe it is a prison cell.
Maybe it is a funeral.
Maybe it is a divorce.
Maybe it is a relapse.
Maybe it is a night when depression almost convinced you to quit.
Maybe it is a prayer whispered through tears.
Maybe it is this very moment.
Whatever place God met you in, never forget it.
Remember it.
Tell the story.
Build the memorial.
Because someone else is still running.
Someone else thinks their scandal is too great.
Someone else believes God could never use them.
Someone else needs to hear what Christ has done in your life.
"Christ is still healing me."
Let your testimony encourage someone who is struggling today.
They may be closer to their Bethel moment than they realize.
Not because salvation can be purchased.
Not because grace has a price.
But because Gospel-centered ministry requires faithful support from believers who want biblical truth to reach more hearts.
Because somewhere right now, another Jacob is lying on a stone, convinced his story is over while God is preparing to rewrite it.
And the place you thought was the end may become the testimony you tell for the rest of your life.
